title: Paxlovid and Alcohol: Can You Drink on It? Risks and Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on Paxlovid? How ritonavir changes other medicines, why alcohol worsens the metallic taste and diarrhea, how long to wait, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Paxlovid? How ritonavir boosts other drugs, alcohol and the metallic taste, COVID recovery, how long to wait, and when to call a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** alcohol is not on Paxlovid's list of drugs you must never combine with it, and there is no known dangerous chemical reaction between the two like the one you get with some antibiotics. But that doesn't make drinking during your five-day course a good idea. Paxlovid contains ritonavir, a booster that slows down how your liver clears a long list of other medicines, and that changes how sleep aids, painkillers, anxiety medicines and some heart drugs behave alongside alcohol. On top of that, alcohol works against your recovery from COVID-19, can make Paxlovid's side effects (metallic taste, diarrhea, nausea) feel worse, and adds work for a liver that is already handling a drug with a liver warning on its label.

**The quick rules:** The simplest and safest plan is to skip alcohol for the five days you take Paxlovid and for about three days after your last dose. If you do have a drink, keep it to one, have it with food, and only if you feel well and take no other sedating medicines. Never combine alcohol, Paxlovid and a sleeping pill, opioid, or anti-anxiety medicine. Before you start, give your pharmacist your full list of medicines and supplements, because most real Paxlovid problems come from other drugs, not from the alcohol itself.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who prescribed your Paxlovid and knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before drinking on Paxlovid if** you have liver disease or have been told your liver enzymes are high, you have kidney disease, you take any prescription medicine (especially for sleep, pain, anxiety, heart rhythm, blood pressure, cholesterol or blood thinning), or you drink most days. **Get urgent care or call 911 if** you have trouble breathing, chest pain or pressure, new confusion, trouble staying awake, bluish lips, yellow skin or eyes, or signs of a serious allergic reaction such as swelling of the face or throat.

## How Paxlovid Works, and Why Ritonavir Is the Part That Matters

Paxlovid is an antiviral pill pack for COVID-19. Each dose combines two different drugs:

1. **Nirmatrelvir.** This is the part that fights the virus. It blocks an enzyme (a protease) that the virus needs to copy itself.
2. **Ritonavir.** This part does nothing to the coronavirus. Its job is to keep nirmatrelvir in your blood long enough to work. It does that by strongly blocking **CYP3A4**, the main liver enzyme that would otherwise break nirmatrelvir down quickly.

The standard course is twice a day for five days, started within five days of symptoms. People with reduced kidney function get a lower dose, which is why your prescriber asks about your kidneys.

Ritonavir is the reason Paxlovid has such a long interaction list. CYP3A4 doesn't just process nirmatrelvir. It also clears a large share of common medicines. When ritonavir blocks it, those other drugs can build up to much higher levels than intended. Some of them are risky enough that the label says not to take them with Paxlovid at all.

### Where alcohol fits in

Your body breaks down alcohol mainly with a different set of enzymes: **alcohol dehydrogenase** and, especially in regular drinkers, **CYP2E1**. CYP3A4 is not the main route for alcohol. That's why alcohol isn't treated as a classic Paxlovid drug interaction, and why the US prescribing information does not list it as a contraindication.

So the real alcohol concerns on Paxlovid are indirect. They fall into four groups:

- **Stacking with other boosted medicines.** If ritonavir is pushing up the level of a sedating drug you already take, adding alcohol on top can cause much more drowsiness or slowed breathing than either would alone.
- **The liver.** Ritonavir can raise liver enzymes, and the label warns about rare cases of liver inflammation. Alcohol also loads the liver.
- **Side effects that overlap.** Paxlovid's common side effects look a lot like a hangover. Alcohol can make them harder to tell apart and harder to put up with.
- **Your recovery from COVID itself.** Alcohol dehydrates you, disrupts sleep, and dampens parts of the immune response at the exact time your body is fighting an infection.

## Can You Drink on Paxlovid? What the Label and Guidance Say

Here is what you can say with confidence:

- **Alcohol is not a listed contraindication.** The FDA prescribing information focuses on drug interactions through CYP3A4 and does not tell people to avoid all alcohol.
- **There is no disulfiram-type reaction.** Some medicines, such as metronidazole, can cause flushing, vomiting and a racing heart when mixed with alcohol. Paxlovid tablets are not known to do this. (Our guide to [metronidazole and alcohol](/never-hungover/metronidazole-and-alcohol) covers that kind of reaction if you're curious why some medicines come with a strict "no alcohol" sticker.)
- **There are no good studies of people drinking while on Paxlovid.** Clinical trials didn't test it. That means nobody can tell you exactly how much is "safe." Anyone giving a precise number is guessing.
- **The label does carry a liver warning.** Ritonavir has been linked with raised liver enzymes, hepatitis and jaundice. Paxlovid isn't recommended in people with severe liver impairment.

Put together: a single drink is unlikely to cause a dangerous reaction in a healthy adult who takes no other interacting medicines. But the potential downsides are real, the upside is close to zero, and you're only being asked to hold off for about a week. Most pharmacists will tell you that skipping it is the easy call.

## The Real Danger: Alcohol Plus Other Medicines That Paxlovid Boosts

If you remember one section of this article, make it this one. The serious problems people run into on Paxlovid nearly always involve a third drug.

Ritonavir can raise the blood level of many sedating medicines. Alcohol is also a sedative. Put them together and the effects add up, sometimes dangerously. Categories to be careful with include:

- **Sleeping pills and sedatives.** Some, such as oral midazolam and triazolam, are not to be taken with Paxlovid at all because their levels can rise sharply. Others need a dose change or a pause.
- **Anti-anxiety medicines.** Several benzodiazepines are processed through CYP3A4. Higher levels plus alcohol means more sedation and slower breathing.
- **Opioid painkillers.** Drugs such as oxycodone and fentanyl are processed by CYP3A4. Higher opioid levels plus alcohol raises the risk of dangerous breathing problems.
- **Some heart rhythm and blood pressure medicines.** Ritonavir can raise levels of certain calcium channel blockers and anti-arrhythmics. Alcohol also lowers blood pressure, so dizziness and fainting become more likely.
- **Certain cholesterol medicines.** Simvastatin and lovastatin are not to be taken with Paxlovid. Others, such as atorvastatin, may need to be paused. (See our [statins and alcohol](/never-hungover/statins-and-alcohol) guide for how those drugs and drinking interact more generally.)
- **Erectile dysfunction drugs.** Sildenafil and similar medicines can build up and lower blood pressure further, and alcohol does the same.
- **Some blood thinners, seizure medicines and immunosuppressants.** These can need careful adjustment, and some seizure medicines make Paxlovid itself less effective.

This is not a complete list. The full interaction table runs to many pages, which is why your pharmacist should check every medicine and supplement you take, including over-the-counter sleep aids and herbal products. St. John's wort, for example, is not to be combined with Paxlovid because it can make the antiviral stop working.

If your prescriber told you to pause one of your regular medicines during Paxlovid, follow that exactly, and don't try to "replace" it with a drink to help you sleep or relax. For a wider view of how alcohol interacts with common prescriptions, see our [alcohol and medications guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-medications).

## Paxlovid Metallic Taste and Alcohol

The most famous Paxlovid side effect is a bitter or metallic taste, sometimes called "Paxlovid mouth." In the main clinical trial, altered taste was the most commonly reported side effect, and many people who take the drug notice it. It usually starts soon after the first doses and fades after the course ends.

People sometimes ask whether a drink will cover up the taste. In practice, it often goes the other way. Many people find that wine, beer and spirits taste off or unpleasant while the metallic taste is active, and alcohol also dries out your mouth, which tends to make bad tastes linger. There's no evidence that alcohol makes the taste change last longer, but there's also no reason to think it helps.

Things that people commonly find more useful for Paxlovid mouth:

- Sipping water often and keeping your mouth moist
- Sugar-free gum, mints, or sour candies
- Brushing your teeth and tongue, or rinsing with a mild mouthwash
- Cold or citrusy foods and drinks
- Plastic cutlery if metal makes the taste worse

The taste is annoying but harmless. If it's so strong you can't eat or drink enough fluids, tell your pharmacist rather than stopping the course on your own.

## Alcohol, Diarrhea and Nausea on Paxlovid

Diarrhea is another of Paxlovid's more common side effects, and some people also get nausea or an upset stomach. Alcohol irritates the gut lining and pulls water out of your body. Combine the two while you're also running a fever or not eating much, and dehydration can sneak up on you fast.

This matters more than it sounds. Being dehydrated makes headaches, dizziness and fatigue worse, and in people with weak kidneys it can raise the level of nirmatrelvir in the blood. If you're having loose stools on Paxlovid, water and an electrolyte drink are what your body needs, not a beer. Our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) explains why alcohol upsets the gut in the first place.

## Does Alcohol Slow Down COVID Recovery?

Paxlovid is meant to lower the risk of a COVID infection getting severe. Alcohol doesn't stop the drug from working against the virus, as far as anyone knows. But it does several things that work against getting better:

- **It weakens parts of the immune response.** Research on alcohol and immunity shows that heavy drinking, and even a single episode of binge drinking, can temporarily blunt how immune cells respond. Our [alcohol and the immune system](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-immune-system-complete-health-impact-2025) guide goes into the details.
- **It wrecks sleep quality.** Alcohol might help you fall asleep, but it fragments sleep in the second half of the night and cuts down on deep, restorative stages. Sleep is one of the most useful things your body has for fighting off an infection.
- **It dehydrates you.** Fever, sweating and a poor appetite already drain fluids. Alcohol adds to the loss.
- **It masks warning signs.** Being tipsy or hungover can make it harder to notice that you're getting short of breath, more confused or more exhausted than you should be. Those are exactly the signs that mean you need care.
- **It can irritate the airways.** Some people find alcohol triggers coughing or makes congestion feel worse.

There's no good evidence that a single drink makes a big difference to your COVID outcome, and you shouldn't panic if you had one before you knew you were sick. But the overall direction is clear: alcohol makes the job of recovering a little harder, at a time when you want everything working for you.

## How Long After Paxlovid Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period for alcohol after Paxlovid. What we do know is how long ritonavir's effect on CYP3A4 lasts. After your last dose, the blocking effect fades gradually over a few days, and drug-interaction guidance usually treats it as lasting about **three days** after the final dose. That's why prescribers often tell people to wait a couple of days or more before restarting a medicine that was paused.

A sensible approach:

| Situation | General guidance |
|---|---|
| You take no other medicines and feel well | Waiting until your course is finished and you feel recovered is a reasonable plan. Many people wait an extra 2 to 3 days. |
| You take any sedating medicine (sleep, anxiety, pain) | Wait at least 3 days after your last Paxlovid dose, and longer if your doctor paused or changed a medicine. Ask your pharmacist. |
| Your doctor paused a regular medicine | Follow their restart instructions first. Don't drink until you're back on your normal routine and feel fine. |
| You have liver disease or raised liver enzymes | Ask your doctor before drinking at all. |
| You still feel unwell or tested positive again | Hold off. Your body is still recovering. |

One more thing: some people get "COVID rebound," where symptoms come back a few days after finishing Paxlovid. If that happens, treat yourself as sick again and skip alcohol until you're better.

## Can You Drink the Night Before Starting Paxlovid?

Paxlovid needs to start within five days of your first symptoms, so many people get the prescription after a day or two of feeling unwell. If you had a drink or two before you found out you were sick, that isn't a reason to delay starting the medicine. Take Paxlovid as prescribed. Start drinking water, eat something, and skip any more alcohol from that point on.

If you had a heavy night of drinking and are now starting Paxlovid, mention it to your pharmacist, especially if you feel very unwell or take other medicines. They can check whether anything else needs adjusting.

## What If You Already Drank on Paxlovid?

Don't panic. For a healthy adult who takes no other interacting medicines, one or two drinks during a Paxlovid course is unlikely to cause a dangerous reaction. What to do:

- **Don't skip or double your next dose.** Take Paxlovid at the normal time.
- **Drink water and eat something.** This helps with both the alcohol and any stomach side effects.
- **Don't add sleep aids or sedating antihistamines tonight.** Let the alcohol clear first.
- **Watch for unusual symptoms** such as extreme drowsiness, confusion, fainting, severe vomiting, or yellowing of your skin or eyes.

If you took Paxlovid, drank, and also took a sedating prescription medicine, call your pharmacist or a poison center (1-800-222-1222 in the US) for advice even if you feel okay. If the person is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or confused, call 911.

## When to See a Doctor

**Get urgent care or call 911 for:**

- Trouble breathing, or breathing that's getting worse
- Chest pain or pressure that doesn't go away
- New confusion, or trouble waking up or staying awake
- Bluish or grayish lips, skin or nail beds
- Swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat, a widespread rash, or hives (possible allergic reaction)
- Someone who has been drinking and is very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, or vomiting while drowsy

**Call your doctor or pharmacist soon if:**

- You notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, pale stools, or pain under your right ribs
- You can't keep fluids down because of nausea, vomiting or diarrhea
- You feel faint or dizzy every time you stand up
- You're not sure whether one of your regular medicines is safe with Paxlovid
- Your symptoms return after you finish the course

## Who Should Be Most Careful

The alcohol question matters most if you:

- Take **any prescription medicine**, especially for sleep, anxiety, pain, heart rhythm, blood pressure, cholesterol, blood thinning, seizures or transplant/immune conditions
- Have **liver disease**, hepatitis, fatty liver, or a history of raised liver enzymes
- Have **kidney disease**, since your Paxlovid dose and fluid needs may be different
- Are older or have a condition that put you at high risk from COVID in the first place (which is usually why Paxlovid was prescribed)
- Usually drink **most days**, since a sudden question of "can I skip a week?" is worth raising honestly with your doctor

If you drink heavily every day and stopping abruptly makes you feel shaky, sweaty, anxious or unwell, tell your doctor. Stopping suddenly after long-term heavy drinking can cause withdrawal symptoms that need medical care, and that's something they can help you plan around safely.

For a broader look at medication safety with supplements and alcohol, our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) is a good next read.

## What About Supplements, Including DHM, While on Paxlovid?

Because ritonavir affects so many drugs, the general advice is to tell your pharmacist about every supplement you take, not just prescriptions. Some herbal products, such as St. John's wort, are not to be combined with Paxlovid. Many others simply haven't been studied with it.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that people use around drinking. There are no studies of DHM taken together with Paxlovid, and no good evidence about how the two might interact. Since your Paxlovid course is short, the simplest choice is to pause DHM and other non-essential supplements for those five days and a few days after, unless your pharmacist says otherwise. DHM is not a treatment for COVID, and it doesn't make it safer to drink while on Paxlovid.

Once you're well and off the medicine, if you're the kind of social drinker who wants something in your routine for nights out, DHM is worth knowing about honestly. The research on it is promising but early: most of it comes from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data. There is no good evidence that it stops hangovers outright, and it's no substitute for drinking less, eating, and staying hydrated. If you want to try it, two widely used options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically take it, and our [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) guide covers the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol is not a listed contraindication for Paxlovid, and it doesn't cause a disulfiram-type reaction.
- The real risks come from **ritonavir boosting other medicines**, especially sedatives, opioids and some heart drugs, and from alcohol adding to their effects.
- Alcohol can worsen Paxlovid's side effects (metallic taste, diarrhea, nausea), add load to your liver, and make COVID recovery a little harder.
- The simplest plan is no alcohol during the five-day course and for about three days after the last dose.
- If you already had a drink, don't panic, don't change your dose, and watch for unusual symptoms. Call a pharmacist or poison center if you also took a sedating medicine.
- Give your pharmacist your full list of medicines and supplements before starting Paxlovid. That's the step that prevents the most problems.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Paxlovid?**

Alcohol isn't a listed contraindication for Paxlovid, and it doesn't cause a disulfiram-type reaction. But the ritonavir in Paxlovid boosts many other medicines, alcohol can worsen side effects like diarrhea and nausea, and it can make COVID recovery harder. The simplest plan is to skip alcohol for the five-day course and about three days after. If you take any sedating medicine, have liver disease, or drink most days, ask your doctor or pharmacist first.

**Is there a direct interaction between Paxlovid and alcohol?**

There is no well-known direct interaction. Paxlovid's interactions mostly come from ritonavir blocking CYP3A4, a liver enzyme that isn't the main route for breaking down alcohol. The concern is indirect: alcohol adds to the effects of sedating drugs that ritonavir can push to higher levels, and both alcohol and ritonavir put some load on the liver.

**How long after finishing Paxlovid can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period. Ritonavir's effect on drug-processing enzymes fades over a few days after the last dose, and interaction guidance usually treats it as lasting about three days. Waiting until you feel recovered and two to three days have passed is a reasonable approach. If your doctor paused one of your regular medicines, follow their restart instructions before drinking.

**Does alcohol make the Paxlovid metallic taste worse?**

Many people find drinks taste off or unpleasant while they have the metallic taste, and alcohol dries the mouth, which tends to make bad tastes linger. There's no evidence it makes the taste change last longer. Water, sugar-free gum, mints, sour candies and brushing your tongue are more commonly helpful. The taste usually fades after the course ends.

**I had a drink on Paxlovid. What should I do?**

For a healthy adult who takes no other interacting medicines, one or two drinks is unlikely to cause a dangerous reaction. Don't skip or double your next dose, drink water, eat something, and avoid sleep aids that night. If you also took a sedating prescription medicine, call your pharmacist or Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US). Call 911 if someone is very hard to wake, confused, or breathing slowly.

**Does alcohol make Paxlovid less effective?**

There's no good evidence that alcohol stops Paxlovid from working against the virus. Some other substances, such as certain seizure medicines and St. John's wort, can reduce Paxlovid's levels, which is why your pharmacist should see your full list. Alcohol's bigger effect is on your recovery: it dehydrates you, disrupts sleep, and can dampen parts of the immune response.

**Can I take DHM or other hangover supplements with Paxlovid?**

DHM hasn't been studied together with Paxlovid, so nobody can say how they interact. Because the course is short and ritonavir affects so many substances, the simplest choice is to pause DHM and other non-essential supplements during the course and for a few days after, and to tell your pharmacist about every supplement you take. DHM is not a COVID treatment and doesn't make drinking on Paxlovid safer.

**Is it safe to drink if I get COVID rebound after Paxlovid?**

If your symptoms come back after finishing Paxlovid, treat yourself as sick again and hold off on alcohol until you feel better. Contact your doctor if rebound symptoms are severe or you have trouble breathing.
